newsitem.title: SLOVENIA: Central European leaders gather in Slovenia.
newsitem.headline: Central European leaders gather in Slovenia.

text.p: The presidents of eight central European states arrived at the Slovenian coastal resort of Portoroz on Friday for two days of talks that will focus on European integration.

The presidents of Germany, Italy and Austria, all members of the European Union, were joined by heads of state from the Czech Republic, Hungary, Poland, Slovakia and Slovenia -- former communist states which have made joining the EU and NATO their main foreign policy goals.

The presidents were due to start their first discussion at 1400 GMT in Piran, a small and picturesque seaside town about three kilometres from Portoroz. Some bilateral meetings have already taken place.

On Friday evening the presidents will attend a concert by Slovenian opera singer Marjana Lipovsek in a Piran monastery. A joint news conference at 0800 GMT on Saturday will be followed by a cruise along the Slovenian coast.
The meeting is taking place 10 days ahead of a EU summit in Amsterdam where leaders are expected to sign a new treaty designed to prepare the 15-member bloc for enlargement into eastern Europe.
"A united, democratic and free Europe is the only good possibility that Europe and Slovenia have," said Slovenian President Milan Kucan, who is hosting the meeting.
The Czech Republic, Hungary and Poland are considered to be the most likely candidates to be included in a first round of EU expansion, with Slovenia figuring as an outside chance.
Bulgaria, Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania and Romania have also applied to join the EU.

The informal two-day summit in Piran, the first significant gathering of heads of state in the former Yugoslav republic, follows similar meetings in Poland last year, Hungary in 1995 and the Czech Republic in 1994.
Analysts said the meeting might prove helpful to Slovenia in its bid to join the EU as soon as possible. Prime Minister Janez Drnovsek has pinned his hopes on entry by 2002.

"The meeting may help towards closer ties between Europe and Slovenia. I expect President Kucan will use it to lobby for Slovenia's inclusion in the first round of the EU and NATO expansion," an analyst said.
While most of the presidents have few political decision-making powers, they are likely to use their influence to try to back the bids of their regional neighbours.

The Czech Republic, Hungary and Poland are almost certain to be invited to join NATO at its summit in Madrid in July but officials said the talks in Piran were not expected to focus on the expansion of the military alliance.
